section.title: Conic sections
section.p: Circles, parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas look like different curves. But they belong to one family.
One way to discover them is to slice a cone. A horizontal slice gives a circle. A slanted slice may give an ellipse, a parabola, or a hyperbola.
There is another way, better suited to calculus and polar coordinates: compare distances.
A conic is controlled by a fixed point and a fixed line.
The curve consists of all points whose distance to the focus has a constant ratio to their distance to the directrix.
That ratio is called the eccentricity.

subsection.p: The value of e determines the kind of conic.

A circle is the perfectly symmetric special case of an ellipse. In the usual two-focus description of ellipses, a circle has eccentricity e=0. The focus-directrix description above is most useful for e>0.

exercise.title: What single comparison produces the whole conic family?

statement.p: A conic is the set of points whose distance to a focus has a constant ratio to their distance to a directrix. In your own words, why does that one comparison unify parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas, and what role does the eccentricity e play?

hint.p: The ratio is e. The cases e<1, e=1, and e>1 distinguish ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.

exercise.title: Why do polar coordinates put every conic in one equation?

statement.p: With the focus at the pole, conics take the form r=p/(1+e\cos\theta). In your own words, why is that a natural language for the focus-directrix definition, and how does the single number e become visible in the formula?

hint.p: Polar coordinates measure distance from the focus directly. After the constant term in the denominator is 1, the coefficient of cosine or sine is the eccentricity.

subsection.p: The polar form
makes eccentricity visible. The single number e decides whether the orbit closes, opens into a parabola, or splits into hyperbola branches.

That fact is more than geometry. It is one of the reasons polar coordinates are central in astronomy and mechanics. Planetary orbits are conics with the sun at a focus. The same polar equation that classifies conics will become an orbit equation.
The next optional project follows that thread. It asks why an ellipse is the natural curve for a planet, and why equal areas swept out by the radius vector correspond to equal times.

exercise.title: When is a Cartesian standard equation the better language?

statement.p: Standard equations such as x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1 put a center at the origin, while polar form puts a focus at the pole. In your own words, why might you choose one description or the other?

hint.p: Cartesian form is convenient for axes of symmetry and translations of the center. Polar form is convenient when the important point is a focus, as in an orbit.
